tagline: A rising band, a Beijing stadium and an Emmy-winning dragon.
headline: Against The Current's Worlds 2017 anthem became a stadium spectacle, a career-maker and a nearly 800-million-stream hit.
summary: Released on September 14, 2017 for the first World Championship held in China, "Legends Never Die" gave Against The Current, then a rising pop-punk trio, the job Imagine Dragons and Zedd had done before them. At the final in Beijing's Bird's Nest, Chrissy Costanza sang it in front of nearly 50,000 fans while an augmented-reality Elder Dragon swooped through the stadium on the broadcast, a show that won Riot a Sports Emmy. Nine years on it has about 788 million Spotify plays, roughly 585 million views across its two League channel uploads and an RIAA Gold certification, and it keeps bringing Costanza back to the Worlds stage.

story.heading: A rising band gets the biggest stage
story.body:
By 2017 the Worlds anthem was a tradition with a big-name guest list: Imagine Dragons wrote *Warriors* in 2014, Nicki Taylor sang *Worlds Collide* in 2015 and Zedd made *Ignite* in 2016. For the seventh World Championship, the first held in China, Riot picked Against The Current, a pop-punk trio from New York made up of singer Chrissy Costanza, guitarist Dan Gow and drummer Will Ferri.

The band were not stars on that scale yet. Costanza later told Esports Insider she assumed the song would be "limited" because of it. They were, however, genuine League people. Costanza had been introduced to the game by musician Alex Goot, who also did additional vocal production on the track, and Riot's making-of video stresses that the band were gamers and that Costanza played and streamed League herself.

story.heading: From a piano sketch to a stadium brief
story.body:
The song started inside Riot. Composer Sebastien Najand made a few instrumental demos and sent Mako's Alex Seaver a chord progression and a bit of piano. Seaver wrote a verse within hours and sent it back that night, and the answer was simply to keep going. Justin Tranter joined as a co-writer, production was shared by the Riot Games Music Team, Seaver and Oliver, and Colin Brittain worked on the vocals. In the making-of, the team says they knew the song was special as soon as they heard Costanza's voice.

The brief was clear. The song was meant to capture the struggle champions go through to become legends, and what it feels like to stand at center stage at Worlds with 50,000 people around you and millions more watching online. Costanza said she pictured a real, physical battle while recording.

Riot released it as an official audio upload on the League of Legends YouTube channel on September 14, 2017, nine days before the tournament began, and as a single the next day. The cover art hid Ashe and Lee Sin inside the silhouette of a player. Polygon called it the Worlds theme players had been waiting for, a song that "encompasses how epic Worlds is."

story.heading: Champions in training, then an Alan Walker remix
story.body:
The animated music video arrived on October 18, midway through the tournament. Earlier Worlds videos had followed players, but this one followed three of League's most familiar champions as they trained: Ashe stalking through a snowstorm with her crystal bow, Lee Sin fighting in a stone training ring, and Garen drilling and sparring with Demacian soldiers. It opens with a player walking down a tunnel toward the Worlds stage and closes on an aerial shot of Beijing National Stadium, where the final would be played. Polygon pointed out the switch from players to champions and the new animation style, and found the result inspiring.

On October 31 Riot added an official remix by Norwegian producer Alan Walker, with vocals from Costanza and Seaver. Billboard heard it as a bright, bouncy take on an anthemic original, a little tropical, with a hook like a half-time hardstyle tune.

story.heading: A dragon in the Bird's Nest
story.body:
The final on November 4, 2017 was held at Beijing National Stadium, the Bird's Nest that had hosted the opening ceremony of the 2008 Olympics. Before Samsung Galaxy and SK Telecom T1 took the stage, Jay Chou performed his Worlds song *Hero*. Then Against The Current played *Legends Never Die* for nearly 50,000 fans, with Chou at the piano.

Midway through, the broadcast showed something the people in the stands could not see. An augmented-reality Elder Dragon landed on the rim of the stadium, swooped low over the crowd, settled on the stage to roar, and took off again as the Summoner's Cup rose. Only broadcast viewers could see it, so fans in the stadium followed it on the giant screens. The dragon was made by Passion Republic. The ceremony's team, which included New Zealand designer Robin Rawstorne, had laser-scanned the stadium about six months earlier and planned the show, with at least 200 performers, inside a 3D model of the venue.

When the games began, Samsung Galaxy swept three-time champions SKT T1 3–0. Tencent reported 60 million unique viewers for the Beijing final, up from 43 million the year before. The closing ceremony brought Alan Walker and Against The Current to the stage together.

story.heading: An Emmy, and a new kind of opening ceremony
story.body:
In May 2018 the broadcast won Outstanding Live Graphic Design at the 39th Sports Emmy Awards. Idealog reported that it was the first time an esports event had won a Sports Emmy. LoL Esports' own upload of the performance calls the dragon's flight a legendary League moment, and it has about 24.4 million views.

The dragon also set a pattern. In 2019 ESPN's Tyler Erzberger likened Riot's Worlds ceremonies to the Super Bowl halftime show, a comparison Riot's Toa Dunn made himself, and traced how each one raised the bar with new technology: the swooping dragon in 2017, K/DA's augmented-reality debut in 2018 and True Damage in 2019.

story.heading: The song that changed Chrissy Costanza's career
story.body:
ESPN wrote that the Bird's Nest performance changed Costanza's life. She remembered so much energy in the stadium that it felt like too much, and said she had to center herself and tune out the crowd to get through it. In 2025 she told Esports Insider she was still stunned by how far the song travelled. She has friends who knew *Legends Never Die* without knowing anything about League of Legends, and who found the game through it. The AU Review credits the song with raising the band to fame.

Riot kept calling. Costanza sang *Phoenix*, the Worlds 2019 anthem, with Cailin Russo. Against The Current recorded *Wildfire* with the LEC in 2022, and by Worlds 2025 Costanza had stood on the Worlds stage more times than any other singer, according to Esports Insider. When NME covered *Wildfire*, it still called *Legends Never Die* an incredible, stadium-sized anthem.

story.heading: Numbers that never die
story.body:
The music video has about 317.9 million views, and the original official-audio upload has another 267.1 million, roughly 585 million across the two League channel uploads. Among Worlds anthem videos, only *Warriors* (457.2M) and *RISE* (425.3M) have more views than the *Legends Never Die* music video. Even the static audio upload outdraws every other Worlds anthem video apart from those two, including *Phoenix* (182.9M). On Spotify the track had about 787.6 million plays by October 8, 2026, second only to *Enemy* on League of Legends' artist page.

Certifications followed: Gold from the RIAA in February 2022, Gold in Denmark, Italy and Spain in 2024, then Platinum in New Zealand and Gold in the UK in 2026. Critics keep it near the top of their rankings. esports.gg's staff ranking put it at No. 1 among Worlds songs, and Esports Insider put it in its top three in 2025, behind *Warriors* and *RISE*.

story.heading: Montages, living rooms and a medley in Chengdu
story.body:
Away from Riot's channels, the song became the soundtrack of League's highlight culture. WeCoach calls it the go-to track for creators showing off their mechanics, whether in an impressive Shurima Shuffle or a hilarious Neeko Pop Blossom fail. In 2021, when Worlds was played in Reykjavík with no crowd, an LPL fan filmed himself performing it at home with his father on French horn and his mother on violin; ONE Esports, covering the clip, pointed out that it was the anthem of the year Worlds was first held in China. The rhythm game *Hextech Mayhem: A League of Legends Story* added it to its "Boombox 2: Zegends Never Die" DLC pack with *RISE* and *Phoenix*. Covers kept coming too, from the symphonic metal band The Dark Side of the Moon in 2023 to Korean rock band N.Flying, who released a medley of *Legends Never Die* and *GODS* on the day of the 2025 final.

That day, November 9, 2025, Costanza opened the Worlds final in Chengdu with a medley of *Legends Never Die*, *Warriors* and *Phoenix*. As in 2017, the reigning champions T1 were waiting behind her. This time they won, becoming the first team to take three World Championships in a row. On April 26, 2026 she sang the song again for T1 fans at the team's Home Ground festival at Inspire Arena in Incheon.

whyItMatters: It turned a rising pop-punk trio into Worlds royalty: the song is credited with Against The Current's rise to fame, and Chrissy Costanza has since appeared on the Worlds stage more than any other singer (2017, 2019, 2025).

Its Worlds 2017 final performance, with an augmented-reality Elder Dragon in the Bird's Nest, won Riot a Sports Emmy for Outstanding Live Graphic Design, which Idealog reported was the first Sports Emmy for an esports event.
That dragon started a run of tech-driven Worlds ceremonies, followed by K/DA's AR debut in 2018 and True Damage in 2019, which ESPN likened to the Super Bowl halftime show.
It is one of Riot's biggest songs: about 585M views across the League channel's music video and official audio, about 788M Spotify plays, RIAA Gold and certifications in five more countries.
Its music video is the third most-viewed Worlds anthem video (after Warriors and RISE), and even its static audio upload outdraws every other anthem video except those two.
It became League's montage music and reached people outside the game. Costanza says some of her friends found League of Legends through the song.
As the anthem of the first Worlds held in China, it carries special weight there, and Riot brought it back to open the 2025 final in Chengdu.

communityMoments.title: The anthem drops
communityMoments.description: Riot released Legends Never Die as an official audio upload on the League of Legends YouTube channel, nine days before Worlds 2017 began. The cover art showed Ashe and Lee Sin inside the silhouette of a player.

communityMoments.title: How it was made
communityMoments.description: Riot's making-of video showed the song growing from a composer's piano sketch and a late-night verse from Mako's Alex Seaver, and introduced Chrissy Costanza as a League player and streamer who mains Annie.

communityMoments.title: Champions in training
communityMoments.description: The animated music video swapped pro players for Ashe, Lee Sin and Garen training to become legends. Polygon noted the new focus and animation style.

communityMoments.title: Alan Walker's remix
communityMoments.description: Alan Walker's official remix, with vocals from Chrissy Costanza and Alex Seaver of Mako, gave the anthem a bright, bouncy dance makeover.

communityMoments.title: The Elder Dragon takes flight
communityMoments.description: At the Worlds 2017 final in Beijing's Bird's Nest, Against The Current performed with Jay Chou on piano while an augmented-reality Elder Dragon swooped over nearly 50,000 fans and roared from the stage.

communityMoments.title: Walker and ATC close the show
communityMoments.description: The final's closing ceremony brought Alan Walker and Against The Current to the stage together for the remix.

communityMoments.title: A Sports Emmy for a dragon
communityMoments.description: The Worlds 2017 broadcast won Outstanding Live Graphic Design at the 39th Sports Emmy Awards.

communityMoments.title: A family cover for the LPL
communityMoments.description: With Worlds 2021 played in Reykjavík without a crowd, an LPL fan filmed himself performing Legends Never Die at home with his father on French horn and his mother on violin.

communityMoments.title: Certified Gold in the US
communityMoments.description: The RIAA certified League of Legends and Against The Current's Legends Never Die Gold.

communityMoments.title: Zegends Never Die
communityMoments.description: The rhythm game Hextech Mayhem: A League of Legends Story added Legends Never Die, RISE and Phoenix in its "Boombox 2: Zegends Never Die" DLC pack.

communityMoments.title: A symphonic metal cover
communityMoments.description: Symphonic metal band The Dark Side of the Moon released a music video for their Legends Never Die cover a month before their debut album Metamorphosis.

communityMoments.title: N.Flying's anthem medley
communityMoments.description: Korean rock band N.Flying released a cover medley of Legends Never Die and GODS on the day of the Worlds 2025 final.

communityMoments.title: Back on the Worlds stage
communityMoments.description: Chrissy Costanza opened the Worlds 2025 final in Chengdu with a medley of Legends Never Die, Warriors and Phoenix, her third Worlds stage appearance. T1, the reigning champions behind her, went on to complete a three-peat.

communityMoments.title: Home Ground in Incheon
communityMoments.description: Costanza sang Legends Never Die, Phoenix and Wildfire in a ten-minute set at T1's Home Ground festival at Inspire Arena.

communityMoments.title: The montage anthem
communityMoments.description: Legends Never Die became the go-to soundtrack for League creators showing off their mechanics, from impressive Shurima Shuffles to hilarious Neeko Pop Blossom fails.

keyMoments.label: Walking out to the Worlds stage
keyMoments.description: A player in a team jacket walks down a dark tunnel lined with Worlds 2017 branding toward the stage lights.

keyMoments.label: Ashe in the snow
keyMoments.description: A hooded Ashe treks through a snowstorm, her crystal bow glowing blue, then looks down on a burning village.

keyMoments.label: Lee Sin's training ring
keyMoments.description: An overhead shot finds Lee Sin alone in the middle of a cracked stone training circle.

keyMoments.label: Garen and the Demacian line
keyMoments.description: Garen marches at the head of a line of Demacian soldiers across a golden field.

keyMoments.label: Into the first chorus
keyMoments.description: Lee Sin balances on a stone pillar as the first chorus builds, then Garen trades blows with Demacian soldiers in a courtyard.

keyMoments.label: Surrounded
keyMoments.description: Echoing the earlier overhead shot, Lee Sin now stands in the training ring surrounded by opponents.

keyMoments.label: Final chorus
keyMoments.description: The last chorus hits as Lee Sin fights his way through a crowd of attackers amid shards of light.

keyMoments.label: Ashe draws
keyMoments.description: In a dark forest, Ashe draws her glowing crystal bow.

keyMoments.label: The arrow flies
keyMoments.description: Ashe looses her arrow. It streaks through the snowy forest and bursts in a flash of ice.

keyMoments.label: Garen faces the army
keyMoments.description: Garen hefts his greatsword and turns toward a vast army on a sunlit plain.

keyMoments.label: Back to the stadium
keyMoments.description: The player steps out in front of a packed arena, then the video cuts to the Bird's Nest under the Worlds logo, where the 2017 final would be played.

keyMoments.label: Alan Walker's drop
keyMoments.description: After the vocal build, Walker's bright, bouncy drop kicks in over the Ashe and Lee Sin cover art.

keyMoments.label: Demos and a late-night verse
keyMoments.description: The writers recall how instrumental demos and a piano chord progression became a verse written in a few hours, with a reply to keep going.

keyMoments.label: Hearing Chrissy's voice
keyMoments.description: The team describes knowing the song was special as soon as they heard Chrissy Costanza sing it.

keyMoments.label: An Annie main
keyMoments.description: Shown playing League, Costanza explains why Annie, the first champion she truly learned, is her main.

keyMoments.label: Center stage at Worlds
keyMoments.description: The brief: what it feels like to stand at center stage at Worlds with 50,000 people around you and millions watching online.

keyMoments.label: Jay Chou at the piano
keyMoments.description: The Bird's Nest performance opens with Jay Chou at a grand piano, accompanying Chrissy Costanza.

keyMoments.label: The Elder Dragon arrives
keyMoments.description: The augmented-reality Elder Dragon lands on the rim of the stadium roof.

keyMoments.label: Over the crowd
keyMoments.description: The dragon swoops low over the packed stands of the Bird's Nest.

keyMoments.label: The roar
keyMoments.description: The dragon settles on the stage and roars at the crowd before flying off as the Summoner's Cup takes center stage.

featuredClip.description: Final chorus: Ashe looses a glowing crystal arrow that streaks through the dark, snowy forest and bursts in a flash of ice.
